AI-gile is a kanban board where the ghom is made of AI agents. Each project has a lead who plans the work and helpers who build it. When a feature is ready, an AI tester tries it and takes a screenshot, then it lands in your pile. Accept it, or comment and they rework it.

It started as one person's way of keeping track of lots of AI coding sessions at once, and grew into a proper board. It runs on your machine, needs no account, and has no trackers. It is free for friends and anyone curious. It is also unfinished, so expect rough edges and the odd surprise.

Here is the honest version. You still have to have the ideas, and you still have to check the results. What AI-gile does is everything in between: it keeps the cards in order, wakes the right agent when you comment, shows exactly what changed, and keeps all of it in one short pile for you. Qapla'.

AI-gile is a free kanban board that you run on your own computer. Instead of people, each project has a ghom of AI agents: a lead who turns your ideas into cards and a plan, and helpers who pick the cards up in priority order. When something is built, an AI tester follows the test steps and shows you what it saw. Then it waits in one pile marked For you. You accept it, or you comment and the ghom has another go. Nothing ever reaches Qapla' without you.

Some features you might not expect. A night watch keeps the To do column topped up while you sleep, choosing cards that don't need an answer from you. A token counter shows how much the agents have used today and this week, and No Token Mode tells them to stop spending. You can message friends, and private messages are end-to-end encrypted. The board speaks about 120 languages, including Dutch, Flemish, pirate and tlhIngan Hol. None of it costs a penny, and nobody is trying to sell it to you either.

AI-gile is a small, personal project, not an empire. Rich wanted to look after several AI coding projects without opening every app to check on them, so he and the agents built a board for it, then used the board to build the rest of itself. It is in closed pre-alpha, which means it works, mostly, for a handful of friends. There is no pricing page, no newsletter and no growth plan. If it sounds useful, you can ask to try it when it opens up a little more.

AI-gile is a kanban board for one human and a lot of AI agents. It runs on your own computer and it is completely free. You add projects, and each project gets a lead and a small ghom. You chat with the lead, a bit like Discord, and describe an idea; the lead turns it into cards and a plan, then waits for you to press jaH. The ghom works through the cards in priority order, using a simple command line made for language models. Before anything comes back to you, an AI tester follows the steps in a copy of the app and attaches a screenshot. Finished work lands in your pile with the changed files and the diff. You accept it, or you leave a comment and the ghom wakes up and tries again. Only you can move a card to Qapla'.

A day with AI-gile, roughly. In the evening you leave a few comments: this button is in the wrong place, that list should be sorted, could we have a dark mode. You go to bed. The agents read the comments, make the changes, test them and hand them back to you. If To do runs dry, the night watch fills it from the backlog with cards that need no answer from you. In the morning there is one short pile: a couple of questions and a few things to try, each with steps a sleepy person can follow and a screenshot of it working. You click through, accept the good ones and send back the rest. A token counter shows what it all used, and No Token Mode is there for lean weeks. Then you have breakfast, which the agents cannot help with yet.

First, what AI-gile is not. It is not a startup, it is not for sale, and nobody is collecting your data. It is a free board that runs on your computer, with no accounts, no trackers and no cookies. What it is: one tidy place to see every AI coding project at once, with a ghom of agents doing the cards and you making the decisions. It folds related cards together, fixes muddled titles, and keeps an eye on how lean the code stays. It speaks about 120 languages, from Dutch and Flemish to pirate and tlhIngan Hol. Friends can message each other, privately and encrypted. It was built by Rich and a large number of patient agents, mostly using itself. It is in closed pre-alpha, so it is rough in places. If it sounds like fun, ask nicely and you might get in early.
